analysis.one_liner: Bars the Department of Homeland Security from buying or using full-body restraints on people in its custody.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban Department of Homeland Security full-body restraints was introduced in February 2026 and has not received a committee vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Homeland Security Act to prohibit the Department of Homeland Security from spending money on, or using, full-body restraints — devices that strap down a person's arms and legs to immobilize them entirely. It would also require quarterly reports to Congress if any restraints are used, naming the restrained individual, the officers responsible, and any injuries, and it would require the firing of any DHS employee who uses one or lies to Congress about it. Contracts signed before the law took effect would be allowed to continue.
analysis.who_benefits: People in DHS custody — primarily immigrants in detention or being transported for removal — gain protection from being immobilized in full-body restraints, a practice that has been associated with serious injury. The public also gains a paper trail: mandatory quarterly reports to Congress naming the restrained individual, the office involved, and any injuries. Taxpayers stop funding acquisition of the devices.

how_it_helps.text: Bars DHS from buying or using four-point and five-point restraints that immobilize a person's whole body.
Requires any DHS employee who uses a full-body restraint, or deceives Congress about it, to be fired.

Requires quarterly reports to Congress detailing every use: who was restrained, their age, race, immigration status, whether they were injured, which office and officers were involved, and what language services were available.

analysis.who_pays: The main cost falls on DHS and its contractors, who lose access to one restraint method; equipment makers lose a federal buyer. Officers dealing with violently resisting detainees would have to rely on other methods, and the saving clause means existing contracts can still run.

drawbacks.text: The saving clause lets the Department keep using full-body restraints acquired under contracts signed before enactment, so the practice could continue indefinitely on existing equipment.

In removal and transport situations where a person is violently resisting, officers would lose a tool they may argue is safer for both the detainee and the officers than alternative force; the bill does not specify what may be used instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—ending a restraint practice that can injure or kill people in government custody—are significant and the fiscal cost is minimal, since the bill mainly bans a purchase and use. The main cost is operational: officers would lose one tool for controlling violently resisting detainees, and the saving clause means existing contracts could keep the equipment in use until expiration. The bill is narrowly drafted and enforceable through mandatory discipline and quarterly reporting, which strengthens it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Homeland Security Committee, which referred it to a subcommittee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Homeland Security Committee.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability, where it has sat.
The bill would amend the Homeland Security Act to bar the DHS Secretary from spending funds on or using four-point and five-point restraints that immobilize a person.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: DHS and its contractors keep the ability to buy and use full-body restraints, and the restraint equipment makers keep their federal market.

for.name: Rep. Delia C. Ramirez
for.role: Sponsor; House Homeland Security Committee member

against.name: House Homeland Security Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action; it was sent to a subcommittee the next day with no hearing or markup scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 16 supporters are Democrats; no Republican cosponsors, and the bill sits in a committee controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill bars DHS from buying or using full-body restraints, eliminating a market segment for makers of such devices. The saving clause lets the Department keep using equipment already under contract, softening the immediate loss.
DHS contractors and detention operators could no longer deploy full-body restraints on detainees in custody or during transports, restricting force practices that have drawn public scrutiny.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no hearing or markup, and a referral only to a subcommittee, the bill is unlikely to advance in this Congress; it would need a committee markup and floor scheduling that the current majority has shown no sign of granting.
